title: How many digits can a product of two numbers have?
description: The smallest and largest products are used to check a claim about two numbers of two digits, and then to answer two more questions about digit counts. Keeko then raises a hand, thinking two numbers of three digits can give four digits.
teaching_notes: One idea: find the smallest and the largest product, count their digits, and every other product lies between them. Ask the class to guess the smallest product of two numbers of two digits before it is written. Watch for students who test only one multiplication and call the claim true or false.

source: Roxie says that the product of two 2-digit numbers can only be a 3- or a 4-digit number. Is she correct?
Can multiplying a 3-digit number with another 3-digit number give a 4-digit number?
Can multiplying a 4-digit number with a 2-digit number give a 5-digit number?
video_script.why: The child has found products of large numbers and read their digits, and now finds the digit count of a product from the smallest and largest products.
video_script.substitution: Take the smallest and largest numbers of the given digit counts, multiply each pair, count the digits, and every other product lies between.
video_script.anchor: The claim of {{NAME_2}} written as a speech card, with the two further questions printed beneath it.
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko says two numbers of three digits each can give a product of four digits. The smallest such numbers are 100 and 100, and 100 × 100 = 10,000 already has five digits.
video_script.payoff_line: Two numbers of three digits never give four digits

final_answer.value: {{NAME_2}} is right; two 3-digit numbers never give 4 digits; a 4-digit times a 2-digit number can give 5 digits (or 6)
final_answer.spoken: {{NAME_2}} is right, two numbers of three digits never give four digits, and a four digit number times a two digit number can give five digits or six digits

names.{{NAME_2}}: Eshwarappa's daughter, who makes the claim about two 2-digit numbers

never_show: the largest product of a 4-digit and a 2-digit number before the answer beat
maths_rules: 2-digit × 2-digit: smallest 10 × 10 = 100 (3 digits); largest 99 × 99 = 9801 (4 digits); every other product lies between, so 3 or 4 digits
video_script.design: One idea: the smallest and largest products fix the digit counts. Wrong idea: Keeko says two numbers of three digits can give four digits. The anchor stays all video; the working band builds in the idea part; no hard clear.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>{{NAME_2}} says that two numbers of two digits give a product of three or four digits.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>We have to check the claim and answer both questions.
<bookmark mark='m1'/>Step one, the smallest number of two digits is ten. Ten times ten is one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>One hundred has three digits.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: largest 2-digit numbers: 99 × 99 = 9801, 4 digits; every product lies between 100 and 9801, so 3 or 4 digits

marks.m3: a bar from 100 to 9801 is drawn with 3 or 4 digits above it

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, the largest number of two digits is ninety nine. Ninety nine times ninety nine is nine thousand eight hundred one.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>That has four digits.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Every other product lies between them, so {{NAME_2}} is right.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: smallest 3-digit numbers: 100 × 100 = 10,000, 5 digits; all other products are bigger

marks.m3: an arrow marks all other products as bigger

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, the smallest numbers of three digits are one hundred and one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Their product is ten thousand, which already has five digits.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Every other product is bigger, so it never has four digits.

marks.m1: 1000 and 10 are written as the smallest numbers
marks.m4: 9,99,900 − 9,999 is written with below 10,00,000 beside it
marks.m5: 5 digits or 6 digits is written under both products

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, the smallest numbers are one thousand and ten, with four digits and two digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Their product is ten thousand, which has five digits, so five digits is possible.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The largest numbers are nine thousand nine hundred ninety nine and ninety nine.
<bookmark mark='m4'/>That product is below ten lakh, so it has six digits.
<bookmark mark='m5'/>A number of four digits times a number of two digits gives five digits or six digits.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Keeko thinks two numbers of three digits each can give a product of four digits.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>But the smallest such numbers are one hundred and one hundred.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>One hundred times one hundred is ten thousand, which has five digits. Every other product is bigger, so four digits cannot happen.
